title: Dan Dan Noodles
subtitle: Sichuan wheat noodles with spiced minced pork and sesame paste
excerpt: Dan dan noodles are a Sichuan street dish of thin wheat noodles topped with a richly spiced mince and dressed with sesame paste, chilli oil and black vinegar. The name comes from the carrying pole vendors used to balance two baskets through the streets. Serves 4 in about 35 minutes.
sourceNotes: Dan dan noodles have been sold on the streets of Chengdu since at least the nineteenth century. The dish is documented in historical accounts of Chengdu street food culture and is described in authoritative detail in Fuchsia Dunlop's 'Land of Plenty' (Michael Joseph, 2001) and 'The Food of Sichuan' (Bloomsbury, 2019). Dunlop notes that the original version contained no sesame paste and was plainer than the more elaborate restaurant versions that became popular outside China.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: The spiced pork mince can be made up to 2 days ahead and reheated. The sauce can be mixed in advance and kept at room temperature. Cook the noodles fresh.

glossaryTerms.definition: A fermented paste made from broad beans and chillies, central to Sichuan cooking. It is salty, deeply savoury and moderately hot. The best variety is Pixian doubanjiang, aged for one to three years. It should be cooked briefly in oil before other ingredients are added to develop its full flavour.

A thick paste made from toasted sesame seeds, darker and more intensely flavoured than tahini. Chinese sesame paste is used in noodle sauces and dressings. If unavailable, a mixture of tahini and a few drops of sesame oil approximates the flavour, though the colour will be paler.

The dried husks of the prickly ash berry, not a true peppercorn. They produce a numbing, tingling sensation on the tongue called ma, which is a defining feature of Sichuan cuisine. They are sold whole or ground and should be toasted briefly before use to develop their floral aroma.

Yibin ya cai is a Sichuan preserved vegetable made from the stems of a mustard plant, salted and fermented. It has a salty, slightly sour flavour and a pleasantly chewy texture. It is sold in small vacuum-sealed packets in Chinese grocery shops and keeps for months once opened and refrigerated.

content.text: This recipe serves 4 and comes together in about 35 minutes. The dish has three components: the noodles, the spiced pork mince cooked with
, chilli oil and soy sauce spooned into each bowl before the noodles go on top.
The sauce goes into the bowl cold, the noodles go on top hot, and the pork goes on top of that. Mix everything at the table just before eating. The
scattered over the pork adds a salty crunch that balances the richness of the sesame. If you cannot find it, finely chopped and drained kimchi gives a similar contrast. Ground
are non-negotiable here: they provide the numbing quality that makes this dish distinctively Sichuan.

Mix the sauce ingredients together in a small bowl, adding the warm water to thin the sesame paste to a pourable consistency. Taste and adjust for salt, heat and sourness. Divide between four serving bowls.
Heat {{vegetable-oil}} in a wok over a high heat. Add the {{pork-mince}} and cook, breaking it up, for 3 to 4 minutes until browned and beginning to crisp at the edges.

Push the mince to one side, add the {{doubanjiang}} to the empty part of the wok and fry for 30 seconds until fragrant and darkened. Stir it into the pork along with the {{soy-sauce}} and {{shaoxing-wine}}. Add the {{ya-cai}} if using. Stir-fry for 1 minute more. Turn off the heat.
Bring a large pot of water to the boil and cook the {{wheat-noodles}} according to the packet instructions. Drain well.

Divide the hot noodles between the four bowls on top of the sauce. Spoon the pork over the noodles. Top with spring onions and crushed peanuts. Bring to the table and mix everything together before eating.

items.symptom: The sauce is too thick and gluey
items.cause: Sesame paste has not been loosened with enough water
items.fix: Add warm water a tablespoon at a time and stir well. The sauce should pour easily and coat a spoon without being stiff.

items.symptom: The pork is watery rather than crispy
items.cause: The wok was not hot enough or the mince was crowded
items.fix: Get the wok properly hot before adding the pork, and do not stir for the first minute. Let it sit and brown before breaking it apart.

items.cause: Doubanjiang and soy sauce are both high in salt
items.fix: Use only 1 tablespoon of doubanjiang and reduce the soy sauce in the sauce. Taste before adding any extra salt at the table.

content.text: Dan dan noodles come from the street food stalls of Chengdu. Vendors carried the noodles and sauce in two baskets hung from a shoulder pole (dan). The dish is now eaten at home across China. Outside Sichuan it is usually milder, with less numbing heat and less vinegar.
